title: Newer isn't always better for washing machines
excerpt: That old top-loader your mother-in-law wants gone is probably more reliable than its replacement. Here's what washing machine repair actually looks like in Connecticut.
author: Elmir R.
content:
I had a woman call me from Glastonbury last spring about her Samsung front-loader throwing an ND error code. Four years old, not draining. The culprit was a seized drain pump — part DC31-00054A, about $35 for the part. Straightforward washing machine repair. But while I was there she mentioned her mother's 2004 Maytag top-loader was sitting in the basement and she was about to donate it. I plugged it in and ran it through a cycle. Thing worked perfectly. I told her that Maytag would probably outlast the Samsung by a solid decade. She wasn't thrilled to hear it. She kept the Maytag.

That visit stuck with me because it's a pattern I keep seeing. The newer machine struggling at year four. The older machine still running at year nineteen. And the customer surprised, because everything they've read tells them newer is better.

What actually breaks — and what it costs

The type of failure tells you almost everything about whether a washing machine repair is worth doing. Older mechanical machines fail mechanically. Newer machines fail electronically. Those two failure types have completely different cost profiles.

Common failures on pre-2012 top-loaders:

  • Lid switch (WP3949247) — about $14, 25 minutes to replace. Machine fills and agitates but won't spin. This is the single most common failure on late-2000s Whirlpool top-loaders.
  • Drive belt — $10 to $20, straightforward swap.
  • Pump impeller — usually something caught in it. $15 to $35 for the part.
  • Inlet valve — $20 to $40, fixes slow-fill or no-fill issues.

These parts have been made by aftermarket suppliers for years and will keep being made because the underlying designs haven't changed. Total repair cost rarely exceeds $110.

Common failures on newer HE front-loaders:

  • Control board failure on a Samsung WF45R6100AW — replacement board alone runs $180 to $240, before I even show up at your door. That machine retailed around $699. You're already at or past the 50% rule on parts alone, on a machine that might be five years old.
  • Door boot seal — see the section below. Not as expensive, but a cost a top-loader never has.
  • Drum bearings — labor-intensive to access on front-loaders. By the time you pay for that work, you're most of the way to a replacement anyway.

That's the core problem with newer high-efficiency washers. When the board goes, the washing machine repair math usually doesn't work. Most of the time I tell people straight: don't fix it.

The efficiency argument has a hole in it

Yes, a modern HE washer uses less water per cycle — somewhere around 13 to 15 gallons compared to 30 to 40 gallons for an older top-loader with a full agitator. That's a real difference. But if you're doing six loads a week in a Connecticut household, you're saving maybe $30 to $50 a year on water depending on your municipal rate.

A $200 board repair at year five wipes out more than four years of those savings in a single afternoon. The efficiency math only works if the machine stays healthy, and a lot of them don't.

Door boot seals and the mold problem

Front-loaders trap moisture in the rubber gasket around the door. On Samsung and LG front-loaders from roughly 2017 to 2021, I've seen a consistent pattern of door boot seal failures showing up around year four or five. The seal — DC64-00802C on several Samsung models — develops micro-tears, harbors mold, and eventually starts letting water past.

Hard water accelerates this. If you're on a well in northern Connecticut, you'll likely see it sooner. The replacement itself isn't terrible, about 45 minutes of work. But it's a cost that a top-loader with a simple hinged lid simply never has.

Parts availability is a real thing nobody mentions at the store

Manufacturers aren't required to stock parts indefinitely. Some brands stop producing electronic components for a specific model within seven years of its last production run. I've had Connecticut customers with machines from 2019 where I couldn't source a control board through any normal channel by 2025.

Meanwhile I can get mechanical components for a 2001 Whirlpool direct-drive transmission from three different aftermarket suppliers by tomorrow morning. That gap doesn't show up in any spec sheet — but it will show up the day you need a washing machine repair and the part simply doesn't exist anymore.

When to fix an older machine — and when to walk away

Fix it if:

  • It's a mechanical failure on a pre-2012 top-loader (lid switch, pump, belt, inlet valve)
  • The repair lands between $60 and $110
  • The machine was originally built to run 15-plus years and has no bearing noise

Walk away if:

  • It's a control board failure on any machine that retailed under $600 — the numbers rarely work regardless of age
  • It's a front-loader with bearing noise at year six or seven — start shopping
  • The repair estimate exceeds 50% of the machine's current replacement cost

Honestly, a used 2005 to 2008 Whirlpool or Maytag top-loader in decent shape can be a smarter buy than a new budget front-loader. When I evaluate one, I listen for grinding on the bearing during spin, check that the agitator dogs are grabbing properly, run the lid switch test, and smell for any burning on the motor during spin. Those are the things that tell you what you're actually buying.

What I'd tell a friend in Connecticut

Don't let a four-year-old machine with a $200 board problem make you feel like washing machine repair is always a bad bet. The math on older mechanical machines is completely different from the math on newer electronic ones. If you're not sure which situation you're in, contact our team and describe the symptom before you do anything. Sometimes it's a $14 part. Sometimes it's a conversation about replacement. We'll tell you which one honestly, because that's what we'd want someone to tell us.

If something's acting up and you want a straight answer, go ahead and book a service call with My Appliance Repair and we'll figure out what you're actually dealing with. If the diagnosis points to a repair that makes sense, we'll do it. If it doesn't, we'll tell you that too.

title: Washing machines that vibrate a lot are draining faster than they should
excerpt: Washing machine vibration usually means a failing bearing — and in Connecticut homes, My Appliance Repair sees this turn into a full drum replacement in under six months.
author: Elmir R.
content:
A washing machine that vibrates hard isn't just annoying. It's telling you something is wearing out, and the longer you wait, the more expensive the repair gets. That's not a general warning — it's a specific mechanical sequence that the technicians at My Appliance Repair see play out on Connecticut service calls more than almost anything else.

What washing machine vibration is actually telling you

One-time thump vs. persistent rumble

There's a difference between a one-time thump from an unbalanced load and a consistent rumble or growl that shows up every spin cycle. The first one is the machine redistributing a clump of wet jeans. The second one is a bearing telling you it's failing. Customers describe it different ways: "sounds like it's got rocks in it," "the whole floor shakes," "there's this grinding noise around 900 RPM." All of them are describing the same thing.

The rear drum bearing is what keeps the drum spinning smoothly on its shaft. When it starts to go, you get washing machine vibration. When it's fully gone, you get metal on metal — and that's when the damage spreads fast.

How vibration connects to drain pump failure

Severe bearing wear doesn't stay isolated to the drum. As the drum wobbles under load, it puts stress on the surrounding components — including the drain pump and its housing. A pump that was draining fine can start underperforming once it's absorbing vibration it was never designed to handle. That's why machines with significant bearing wear often show secondary symptoms: slower draining, residual water in the drum, or the machine taking longer than usual to complete a cycle. The vibration and the drain behavior are connected, even if they look like separate problems.

The seal fails first, then everything else follows

Here's what most people don't know: the bearing seal fails before the bearing does. That seal is what keeps water out of the bearing race. Once it starts weeping, even a little, water mixes with the bearing grease and you get corrosion. A bearing that might have lasted another two or three years goes from "slightly noisy" to completely destroyed in a matter of months.

Customers call and say the noise started about five months ago. By the time we get there, the seal is gone, the bearing is gone, and there's rust staining around the drum shaft behind the door boot. Five months is about average for that progression in Connecticut homes — and basements make it worse, since cooler, damper air accelerates bearing corrosion once a seal starts to go.

On a lot of front-loaders, the spider arm fails at the same time. That's the cast aluminum bracket connecting the drum to the shaft. When washing machine vibration gets bad enough, it stresses the spider arm joints and causes hairline cracks. Parts for a mid-tier spider arm run $55 to $120 depending on brand, and it's a three-hour job minimum because you're pulling the whole drum anyway.

Samsung front-loaders, stated plainly

A real call from Shelton, CT

A customer in Shelton called about her washing machine shaking the whole laundry room. She'd been dealing with it for about five months and figured it was normal for a front-loader. Samsung, 2018. The noise was audible from the driveway during the spin cycle. Pulling the boot seal revealed rust-colored water staining all the way around the drum shaft, and a hairline crack starting on one of the spider arm's three joints.

The quote for outer tub assembly replacement came to parts alone at $310, with labor pushing the total past $500. The machine had maybe $200 of useful life left. The recommendation was straight: this one's done. She bought a Maytag top-loader and hasn't needed a service call since — which is exactly the outcome worth aiming for.

Why Samsung's welded tub changes the math

Samsung front-loaders from roughly 2015 to 2021 have an outer tub that is ultrasonically welded shut. You can't split it to replace the bearing without cutting it, which adds risk and voids any remaining warranty. So when the bearing fails, you're often looking at a full outer tub assembly replacement — and that math almost never works out in favor of repair.

If you have a Samsung front-loader from that era and it's starting to rumble at spin, get someone to look at it now, not in three months. Catching it while the bearing seal is just starting to fail is the difference between a $180 repair and a replacement conversation.

LG and Whirlpool are a different story

LG front-loaders from roughly the same period are more serviceable. The tub comes apart. A rear drum bearing kit for a mid-tier LG runs about $48 in parts, and labor is 1.5 to 2 hours because you're still pulling the drum. The spider arm failure rate on these machines is higher than it should be — showing up around years 5 to 7 — but at least the repair is possible, and the numbers usually make sense if the machine is under 9 or 10 years old.

Whirlpool and Maytag top-loaders are the most forgiving of the three. The transmission and bearing designs are simpler and more accessible, and a bearing swap on a Cabrio-platform machine is a reasonable repair that doesn't require a three-hour teardown.

What we check in the first five minutes

When My Appliance Repair responds to a washing machine vibration call in Connecticut, the diagnostic starts immediately:

  • Drum play test: Grab the drum and push it side to side and front to back. More than about a quarter inch of play points directly to bearing failure.
  • Sound character: Bearings growl. A loose drum baffle knocks. Those are different sounds pointing to different repairs.
  • Boot seal inspection: Pull back the door boot seal and look for rust staining around the drum shaft. That staining reveals how long the seal has been leaking.
  • Drain check: If the vibration has been ongoing, we also verify the drain pump is clearing water at the right rate — bearing-related vibration frequently causes secondary drain symptoms that compound the original problem.

On leveling feet

Leveling matters. If your machine is walking across the floor or banging hard during spin, check the feet first — loosen the lock nut, thread the foot in or out until the machine sits flat, then snug the lock nut back down. That takes five minutes and is worth doing before calling anyone.

But leveling doesn't fix a bearing. If you leveled the machine and it still rumbles at high RPM, the feet weren't the problem.

When repair makes sense

The rough math: if the machine has a serviceable tub design, it's under 8 years old, and no other major systems are failing, a bearing job usually makes sense. Top-loaders in that situation, LG front-loaders in that situation — yes. A Samsung front-loader with a welded tub that's already at 6 or 7 years and a fully failed bearing? The numbers don't work, and it's better to say that at the door than after a diagnostic fee has already been paid.

You can look through our appliance repair services for a sense of what's typically repairable and what we recommend replacing. If you're not sure what you've got, contact our team — we can usually tell you something useful before we even come out.

So if your machine has been rumbling for a few months and you've been hoping it would sort itself out, it won't. title: Stove burners that won't light are usually a $4 fix
excerpt: A gas burner that won't light is usually a dirty cap or trapped moisture — not a costly part. Connecticut homeowners can diagnose it in minutes.
author: Elmir R.
content:
Most of the time, a gas burner that won't light comes down to a dirty ceramic cap or a little trapped moisture — not a failed part. At My Appliance Repair, the calls we get where an actual part is the problem are probably one in five. The other four are something you can handle yourself in under thirty minutes if you know what you're looking at.

Three separate things can stop a gas burner from lighting

The ceramic igniter cap sits directly on top of the burner. It's the little dome-shaped piece, usually white or off-white, that you can lift right off with your fingers. These crack from thermal cycling — the constant heat-up and cool-down over years — and a cracked cap breaks the spark gap just enough to kill ignition. GE and Frigidaire gas ranges from roughly 2012 to 2019 have this problem more than anything else we see, almost always on the front-left burner because that's the one people actually use. A replacement cap runs $8 to $14 depending on brand, and swapping it takes five minutes.

Below the cap is the igniter electrode — a small ceramic post with a metal tip that produces the spark. Grease and food debris pack into the tip and block the spark. This one you clean, not replace. A toothbrush and a little patience usually handles it.

Then there's the spark module, which is the control board that sends voltage out to every igniter on the range. That's the expensive one. On an older Frigidaire slide-in where the spark module is integrated into a larger control board, we've seen parts quotes over $300 for a range that isn't worth $400. Don't fix that. But the module fails a lot less often than people assume, and it's almost never where the diagnosis lands when a gas burner won't light.

Clicking that won't stop is usually not a broken part

If the burner keeps clicking after you release the knob, that's moisture in the igniter well — almost always from a boil-over. Soup, pasta water, anything that spills under the burner cap leaves water sitting on the electrode contacts, and the igniter keeps sparking because it reads that as an unlit burner. It's not broken. It's wet.

Dry it out before you assume anything is wrong:

  • Pull the burner cap off and blot what you can with a dry cloth or paper towel.
  • Set your oven to 170°F for 20 to 30 minutes with the burner area open to the heat.
  • Let everything cool completely, set the cap back on, and try again.

Humidity makes this worse in summer, so if this happens in July and the clicking lingers longer than expected, that's why. Connecticut's humid summers are a surprisingly common reason we get calls about burners that won't light — and the fix is almost always just drying things out. No click at all is a different problem — that points to the electrode or the module, not moisture.

The free diagnostic most people skip

If one gas burner won't light and the others work, pull the igniter cap off the dead burner and swap it with the cap from a working one. Same range, same model — they're interchangeable. Here's what each outcome tells you:

  • Dead burner fires with the working cap: You have a cracked cap. Cost to fix: $8–$14.
  • Dead burner still won't fire: The problem is the electrode or wiring beneath it, not the cap.

Why this swap matters before you call anyone

That one cap swap takes about two minutes and tells you almost everything you need to know. It rules out the most common cause of a gas burner that won't light, and it saves you the diagnostic fee if you do end up calling a technician — because now you can tell them exactly what you've already eliminated.

A Tuesday in Hamden

A homeowner called My Appliance Repair about her front-left burner clicking nonstop for two days. She'd already ordered a new range. We came in, pulled the igniter cap — it was wet from a boil-over two days earlier — dried everything out, and set the cap back on. Burner lit on the first try. She canceled the range order. The visit was 18 minutes, and we barely touched a tool. That's not a rare outcome. That's just what happens when you know what to look for.

Where the cost line actually is

Here's a quick breakdown of what these repairs actually cost in Connecticut:

  • Ceramic igniter cap: $8–$14 in parts, five minutes to swap.
  • Igniter electrode (e.g., GE part WB13K10014): $18–$22 in parts, about 25 minutes labor.
  • Spark module: $90–$160 in parts — and up to $300+ on integrated boards. This is where you call someone, because you're working with line voltage.
  • Gas valve replacement: Licensed repair only. Do not DIY this one.

If your range is over 15 years old and the spark module is gone, price a replacement before authorizing the repair. The math usually doesn't work in the module's favor on an old machine.

title: Refrigerator coils you never clean are costing you real money
excerpt: Dirty refrigerator condenser coils cost Connecticut homeowners up to $14/month in wasted electricity — and can kill a compressor early. Here's how to fix it in 15 minutes.
author: Elmir R.
content:
Last winter we got a call from a homeowner in Milford who was convinced her five-year-old LG French door fridge was dying. Compressor running nonstop, couldn't get below 40°F. She'd already been quoted a compressor replacement by someone else. Before the technician even opened his bag, he popped the front grille off. The refrigerator condenser coils were so packed with dog hair from her two golden retrievers that he could barely see the fins underneath. Eight minutes with a brush. Two hours later the fridge was sitting at 37°F. The compressor quote she'd been given was $480 just for the part.

That's not a fluke. Here at My Appliance Repair, we see a version of that call more than we'd like to.

Where the condenser coils actually are on your fridge

On most modern bottom-freezer and French door units, the refrigerator condenser coils sit behind a grille at the front bottom of the machine. That grille snaps off with no tools — homeowners are genuinely surprised every time we show them. Older top-freezer models — Whirlpool and Maytag from the mid-2010s especially — sometimes have rear-mounted coils on the back of the unit. Those collect a little less debris but still deserve a look every couple of years.

Built-ins and some counter-depth models are a different story. Those can have coils tucked behind a rear access panel that requires partial disassembly to reach. Not a 15-minute job on those. If you're in Connecticut and you're not sure what you're getting into, contact our team before you pull anything apart.

What clogged condenser coils actually do to a compressor

The condenser coils exist to shed heat. When they're matted with dust and pet hair, the compressor can't release heat efficiently — so it runs longer and hotter each cycle to maintain target temperature. Over months, that adds up to roughly $8–14 per month in wasted electricity on a full-size side-by-side, depending on your rate. Over years, it shortens the compressor's life.

A compressor replacement on a mid-range fridge runs $400–600 in parts and labor. If the machine is over 8 years old when it fails, that repair almost never makes financial sense. Dirty condenser coils are a contributing factor in roughly 20–30% of the premature compressor failures we diagnose at My Appliance Repair — not the only cause, but a real one.

The sequence most people miss: skipped maintenance → compressor stress → a repair bill that exceeds the machine's value.

The pet hair problem is worse than you think

Homes with dogs and cats are the worst offenders by a wide margin. We've pulled coil mats off LG French door units that looked like something had nested there. The LG LRMVS3006 series and similar models have bottom-front coil placement with a grille that sits about two inches off the floor — in a house with a shedding dog, those refrigerator condenser coils fill up fast. It's worse if the fridge is on carpet or near a return air vent.

If you have pets and you've never popped that grille off, the first cleaning is going to be the most important one you ever do.

How to clean refrigerator condenser coils in 15 minutes

What you need

  • A condenser coil cleaning brush (the Frigidaire 5303281153 is common — any generic equivalent works fine)
  • A vacuum with a soft brush attachment
  • About 15 minutes

Step-by-step

  1. Unplug the refrigerator before you start. Always disconnect power before working under or behind the unit.
  2. Snap off the front grille at the base of the fridge — no tools needed on most models.
  3. Work the coil brush carefully along the fins without bending them.
  4. Vacuum up what comes loose.
  5. Snap the grille back on, then plug the fridge back in.

The brush costs about $7–9 at any hardware store and lasts for years. Do it once a year as a baseline — every six months if you have pets or the fridge lives in a dusty basement. If the fridge is six or more years old and you've never done this, do it this week.

When to call a technician instead

If your fridge is already running constantly, not holding temperature, or showing heavy frost buildup on the back wall of the freezer, dirty condenser coils may be part of the problem but probably aren't the only thing going on. A clogged coil is a maintenance issue. A fridge that's already symptomatic is a diagnostic call.

Sometimes the damage is already done and the compressor is failing regardless. If cleaning the coils doesn't bring the machine back to normal within a few hours, that's when you want a technician to come look at it properly. You can check out our appliance repair services to get a sense of what that looks like.

Connecticut summers make this worse

Ambient kitchen temperature goes up in July and August, the compressor already works harder to maintain 37°F, and dirty refrigerator condenser coils compound that load directly. Connecticut homeowners feel this most during summer heat waves — it's a year-round maintenance issue, but if you've been putting it off, right now is a reasonable time to stop.

This is one of the few things you can do yourself that has a direct, measurable effect on how long a fridge lasts. Most maintenance advice is vague. This one isn't. Clean refrigerator condenser coils → compressor runs less → compressor lasts longer. That's the whole chain.

If you're already past the maintenance stage and something isn't right, book a service call with My Appliance Repair and we'll come take a look.

title: Your microwave is probably the most ignored appliance in your kitchen
excerpt: Most people ignore their microwave until it breaks — then assume it's trash. A Connecticut appliance tech explains what common repairs actually cost, and when to fix vs. replace.
author: Elmir R.
content:
Most people treat their microwave like a smoke detector: ignore it completely until something goes wrong, then assume the whole thing needs to go. I've been doing appliance repair for 20 years, and the microwave is almost always the last thing customers think about maintaining — and the first thing they're ready to throw out when it acts up. Most of the time, microwave repair is faster and cheaper than they expect — and the fix is usually something simple.

Here are the problems I see most often in Connecticut homes — and what they actually cost to fix:

  • Breaker tripping traced to a door interlock switch (under $90 total)
  • No heat caused by an $8 diode, not a $130 magnetron
  • Thermal shutdowns from a clogged grease filter ($9–$15 fix)
  • Grinding turntable motors that turn into bigger problems if ignored

The tripping breaker that wasn't an electrical problem

A customer in Fairfield called me about a kitchen breaker that kept tripping. She'd had two electricians out before me. They replaced the breaker, checked the wiring, found nothing. She'd been resetting it every few days for two months and figured it was just an old-house thing.

I walked in, pressed the microwave door closed, and watched the breaker trip. Secondary interlock switch. It's one of three door switches on most over-the-range microwaves, and when it fails, it can arc and pull enough current to trip a 20-amp circuit. The switch itself was $14. Total repair was under $90. The two electrician visits had cost her over $300 combined.

LG and Whirlpool OTR units from roughly 2016 through 2021 show this pattern more than I'd like. It's not a design defect exactly, but heavy door use wears the interlock switches faster than most people expect. The fix is almost always under $40 in parts — and it's one of the most satisfying microwave repair calls I go on, because the customer genuinely can't believe how simple it was.

It runs, it hums, it does nothing

The high-voltage diode is an $8–$12 part that converts AC to DC for the magnetron. When it fails, the microwave sounds completely normal. The turntable spins, the light comes on, the fan runs. The food just stays cold. Customers describe it as "it's running but not heating," and most of them have been living with it for weeks, assuming that's just what the microwave does now.

This one gets misdiagnosed constantly because people assume no heat means a dead magnetron. A magnetron is $80–$130 in parts before labor. The diode is $8. They're not the same problem, and the symptoms are nearly identical to someone who doesn't know what to listen for. Catching this early is the difference between an inexpensive microwave repair and a much larger bill — which is exactly why it's worth calling a tech before you assume the worst.

What the grease filter is actually doing

On an over-the-range unit, the grease filter isn't just about smoke and cooking odors. When it clogs, heat backs up into the cavity and trips the thermal cutout on the magnetron. The unit shuts down mid-cycle, resets after a few minutes, and the customer thinks it's glitching. I see this a lot on Samsung OTR units across Connecticut when the filters haven't been touched in a year or more.

Replacement filters run $9–$15 and should be washed every 2–3 months if you cook regularly. Almost nobody does this — and a $12 filter is a lot cheaper than a microwave repair call that could have been avoided entirely.

The grinding noise people ignore for months

When the turntable motor starts dragging, most people just live with the noise. That's a mistake. A turntable motor on a common LG or Whirlpool OTR unit runs $22–$28 in parts and takes about 40 minutes to swap. Let it go long enough and it burns out the coupler assembly too, which turns a straightforward microwave repair into a more involved one. If your tray is grinding or stuttering, get it looked at before it stops moving entirely.

When to repair and when to walk away

Countertop vs. over-the-range: the decision that changes everything

On a countertop unit you bought for $150, don't spend money on major component repairs. If it needs a magnetron or a control board, replace the machine. But an over-the-range microwave is built into your cabinetry and costs $400–$700 to buy and reinstall. On those, almost everything short of a magnetron failure is worth fixing. A door latch assembly runs about $18–$34 in parts and 45 minutes of labor. That's not a reason to gut your kitchen and start over.

How to decide quickly

  • Countertop unit under $200: Skip repairs on anything major — replace it.
  • Countertop unit $200–$400: Door switches, diodes, and turntable motors are worth fixing.
  • Over-the-range unit: Almost any repair short of a magnetron replacement is cost-effective given reinstallation costs.

The countertop vs. OTR distinction is the thing most people miss when they're deciding whether to call a repair shop. At My Appliance Repair, we work on both, and we'll tell you upfront if it's not worth fixing. If you want to review our appliance repair services, that's a good place to start.

One thing that's worth taking seriously

A door that doesn't close flush, or one with visible damage to the seal or the inner glass, isn't just a performance issue. Microwave radiation leakage from a compromised door is a real concern, not a theoretical one. A cracked door or a bent frame that won't seat properly should get looked at — not ignored and not kept running while you figure it out later.

title: Stop running your dishwasher on hot dry
excerpt: Turning off dishwasher heated dry protects door gaskets, heating elements, and control boards — advice from a Connecticut appliance repair tech at My Appliance Repair.
author: Elmir R.
content:
Most people never touch the dishwasher heated dry setting. It ships enabled, they run it that way for six years, and the first time they think about it is when a technician from My Appliance Repair is standing in their kitchen replacing a door gasket. If you're in Connecticut and you've had a dishwasher leak, a failed heating element, or a dead control board, there's a reasonable chance the heated dry setting played a role. Our dishwasher repair team sees this pattern repeatedly across Fairfield County and the rest of Connecticut.

What dishwasher heated dry is actually doing to your machine

After the final rinse, the heating element kicks on and holds the interior at roughly 140 to 145 degrees Fahrenheit for 30 to 45 minutes. That heat evaporates the water — and it also works on every rubber seal, every plastic component, and every wire connection in the door assembly, every single cycle, for as long as you own the machine.

It's not doing any of that damage dramatically. It's doing it slowly, cycle by cycle, in a way you won't notice until something fails.

The heating element itself has a finite number of high-heat cycles before resistance climbs and it starts drawing more current or fails outright. On machines where the same element handles water heating during the wash and then drying afterward, you're running it twice as hard. A replacement heating element on a mid-range KitchenAid or similar runs $45 to $85 for the part, plus about an hour of labor — a repair that shows up earlier than it should on machines where dishwasher heated dry runs every cycle.

The gasket damage heated dry causes — and nobody mentions at purchase

Door gaskets are rubber. Rubber degrades faster with repeated heat exposure, and the failure pattern looks different from normal wear:

  • Normal age compression: gasket flattens and stiffens evenly
  • Heat fatigue from heated dry: small lateral cracks, usually along the bottom corners, where the door flexes slightly every time it opens and closes

By the time those cracks are leaking, the customer has usually been running heated dry for five or more years and has no idea the two are connected.

A real example from Fairfield, Connecticut

We had a customer in Fairfield call My Appliance Repair about her Whirlpool Gold from around 2018 — a slow seep onto the floor after every cycle. The gasket had exactly that heat-cracked look. She ran dishwasher heated dry every cycle because she thought air dry meant the dishes would smell. Gasket was $21. Labor was half an hour. She asked why the manual didn't say any of this. It sort of does — buried in the fine print. They just don't make it obvious.

How Bosch solved the heated dry problem

Bosch dishwashers don't use a traditional heating element for drying. They use condensation drying, which works by making the stainless steel tub cooler than the dishes so moisture migrates to the walls and drains away. No sustained high heat, no element cycling on after the rinse.

Their tubs and gaskets age noticeably better than comparable Whirlpool or GE units, and that's not a coincidence. When Bosch customers complain their dishes aren't "dry enough," they're usually comparing to a heated dry result from a previous machine. The dishes are dry — they're just not hot. That engineering choice wasn't marketing. It was a straightforward answer to the wear problem dishwasher heated dry creates.

The Whirlpool WDF control board pattern

On Whirlpool's mid-tier WDF series dishwashers, there's a higher rate of control board failures when heated dry is combined with a heavy-cycle setting. The board is managing a long wash phase and then a sustained heating phase back to back, and that sustained load shortens its life. Control board replacements run $180 to $400 depending on the model — not a repair anyone wants to quote on a seven-year-old machine.

The energy cost of running heated dry every cycle

Heated dry adds roughly 15 to 20 cents per cycle in electricity. Run the dishwasher daily and that's around $55 to $70 a year, just for the drying phase. Over five years that's over $300 — spent on accelerating the exact wear described above.

The alternative is free: crack the door open two inches at the end of the cycle and walk away for 20 minutes. A few things to keep in mind:

  • Plastic items will still have some water on them — that's physics, not a malfunction
  • Rinse aid handles most of the residual moisture
  • A bottle of Finish Jet-Dry runs about $4 and lasts a couple of months
  • That combination — no heated dry, plus rinse aid, plus cracking the door — is the whole solution for most households

Should you turn off dishwasher heated dry? Yes — here's why

The case for turning it off comes down to three things: component lifespan, energy cost, and the fact that air drying with rinse aid gets you 95% of the same result. There's no scenario where running the heating element for an extra 30 to 45 minutes every cycle is beneficial to the machine. It's a default setting that made sense when rinse aid wasn't widely used — it's less justified now.

If you're in Connecticut and your dishwasher is already showing signs of wear — a soft gasket, longer cycle times, dishes that aren't fully cleaned — those are worth looking at before they become bigger problems. Turning off heated dry won't fix existing damage, but it will slow down what comes next.

A note on Connecticut summers and dishwasher drying

In humid months, Connecticut customers call more often about dishes not drying properly even with heated dry running. Sometimes they respond by selecting a heavier cycle or bumping heated dry to "high." That usually makes things worse. Humidity slows evaporation regardless of setting. Chasing dryness with more heat just adds wear. Open the door, let the steam out, and you're done.

What to do right now if your dishwasher needs attention

Start with the simple fix:

  • Go turn heated dry off today
  • Buy a bottle of rinse aid if you don't already use one
  • Start cracking the door open at the end of the cycle

That's it for prevention. If you're already dealing with a leaking door or a dishwasher that isn't finishing cycles correctly, contact our team and we'll tell you honestly whether it's worth fixing. If you already know you need someone out, go ahead and book a service call with My Appliance Repair and we'll get it sorted out.

title: Cleaning the lint trap isn't enough
excerpt: Dryer lint trap cleaning every load isn't enough. Hidden lint in the blower wheel and trap slot slows dryers — and causes house fires. Connecticut dryer repair.
author: Elmir R.
content:
Dryer lint trap cleaning is a habit most Connecticut homeowners have down cold — pull the screen, peel off the lint, push it back in. But the lint screen catches maybe 70% of what your dryer produces. The fine particulate that slips through keeps moving: coating the inside of the trap slot, sticking to duct walls inside the cabinet, and packing itself into the blower wheel. After three to five years of regular use, that buildup is substantial. And nobody cleaned it because nobody knew to look there.

According to the U.S. Fire Administration, clothes dryers cause roughly 2,900 home fires every year. Most people point to the vent duct — but a significant share trace back to internal lint restriction that basic dryer lint trap cleaning never reaches.

The screen is only the first filter in a longer path, and what it misses creates the real problem — one we diagnose on dryer calls across Connecticut every week.

Why dryer lint trap cleaning is only half the job

Most homeowners treat dryer lint trap cleaning as a single step: remove the screen, peel off the visible layer, replace it. That habit is worth keeping. But the trap slot the screen lives in — and the blower wheel the airstream feeds into — are collecting lint the whole time, invisibly. Those two areas are where the real restriction builds, and neither one cleans itself.

Pull your lint screen out right now and look at the slot it lives in. Run your finger along the side walls. There's a felt-like gray layer built up in there, and it narrows the airflow opening whether or not your screen is spotless. A narrow, flexible dryer lint brush costs about $8 at any hardware store. That slot should get brushed out every three to six months. Most people do it never.

Where lint actually goes after the screen

Airflow in a dryer runs drum to lint screen to blower wheel to exhaust duct. Anything small enough to get past the screen rides the airstream straight into the blower housing. The blower wheel — the fan that actually pulls air through the machine — has fins designed to move air. Those same fins are perfect for catching fine lint. Over time they cake up, the wheel moves less air, and the dryer runs hotter and slower trying to compensate.

The trap slot compounds the problem. Even with consistent dryer lint trap cleaning at the screen level, the slot walls narrow over time. Brushing them out takes five minutes and costs nothing beyond the brush. It's the most overlooked maintenance step on any dryer.

The blower wheel: what restricted airflow actually looks like

We pulled a Whirlpool dryer for a customer in Milford last year. She'd had her exhaust vent professionally cleaned six months before, so she ruled that out and figured the heating element was going. We pulled the back panel off, ran the machine for two minutes, and watched the blower wheel barely turn. It was so packed with lint it had almost no clearance. The heat was building up inside the cabinet because air had nowhere to go fast enough.

We cleared the wheel, brushed out the slot, put the panel back on. She ran a full load of towels in 47 minutes. Parts: nothing. Her dryer had been limping along for almost a year, running two full cycles per load, because of internal lint buildup she didn't know to address.

Whirlpool and Maytag dryers from roughly 2015 to 2022 are the machines we open up most often with this problem. The exhaust path routing on those models pulls lint past the screen faster than some other designs. Samsung gas dryers from the same era show it too, sometimes faster. If we do ten dryer calls in a week across Connecticut, two or three of them trace back to internal lint restriction — not a failed component.

The thermal fuse that keeps blowing

On Whirlpool machines, the thermal fuse is part number 3392519. It costs about $6. It's a one-time safety device that cuts power to the heating circuit when the dryer gets too hot. When airflow is restricted by a packed blower wheel, temperatures inside the cabinet climb, and the fuse blows to protect the machine. That's the fuse doing exactly what it's supposed to do.

But here's the pattern we see constantly. Customer replaces the fuse, dryer works, fuse blows again four to six months later. They replace it again. Now they think the dryer is dying. It's not. The fuse is a symptom. The restricted airflow is the cause. Until you fix the airflow — which means going beyond basic dryer lint trap cleaning to the blower wheel itself — you'll keep buying fuses.

What you can do yourself — and what you probably can't

DIY: cleaning the lint trap slot

The lint slot is a genuine DIY job. Here's how to do it:

  • Pull the lint screen completely out of the slot
  • Insert a flexible dryer lint brush into the slot and work it down both sides
  • Pull out whatever the brush brings up — the first pass after a few years will surprise you
  • Repeat every three to six months to keep it manageable

This takes about five minutes and costs nothing beyond the brush. It's the single most overlooked maintenance step on any dryer, and it's something every Connecticut homeowner can do without touching a panel or a wire.

Professional: cleaning the blower wheel

The blower wheel is a different story. Getting to it usually means removing the front or rear panel depending on the brand, disconnecting a few wires, and knowing what you're looking at once you're in there. If you're comfortable with basic appliance disassembly, it's manageable. If you're not, don't guess. A clogged blower on a machine that's otherwise fine is a $45 to $85 parts job if the wheel needs replacing, plus labor — and it's worth doing right.

At My Appliance Repair, we handle this regularly for homeowners across Connecticut who assumed their dryer needed a new part when all it needed was a thorough cleaning. You can book a service call and we'll tell you honestly what we find.

Don't replace the heating element until you've checked airflow

A heating element on a standard electric dryer runs $30 to $55 in parts, and it's a reasonable fix when the element has actually failed. But a clogged blower wheel mimics a bad element symptom-for-symptom:

  • Long drying times even on high heat
  • Clothes still damp at the end of a full cycle
  • Heat that feels weaker than it used to
  • Dryer running multiple cycles to finish one load

We've seen Connecticut customers spend money on a new element and have the exact same problem a month later because nobody checked the blower. The part didn't fix it. The airflow did — and in most of those cases, cleaning the internal components was the only repair needed.

If your dryer has been running slow for more than a few months and a vent cleaning didn't solve it, contact our team or have someone pull the panel and check the blower before you buy anything. It's usually faster to diagnose than people expect.

Connecticut dryer repair: what we see in the field

We service dryers across Connecticut — from Fairfield County up through Hartford and into the shoreline towns. The call volume on slow, overheating dryers spikes every fall when households start running heavier loads. The overwhelming majority of those calls are not mechanical failures. They're maintenance problems: lint where it shouldn't be, airflow that's half what it should be, and a machine that was never told to do anything except run.

Towns like Milford, Shelton, Derby, and Ansonia send us a steady stream of Whirlpool and Samsung dryers with exactly the blower restriction described above. New Haven and Hamden calls trend toward older Maytag units where the slot hasn't been brushed in five or more years. The geography changes the brand mix slightly — the root cause almost never changes.

If you're in Connecticut and want My Appliance Repair to take a look, schedule a repair and we'll sort out what's actually going on.

Frequently asked questions

How often should I clean more than just the lint screen?

Brush out the lint trap slot every three to six months. The blower wheel should be inspected every two to three years, or sooner if you notice drying times increasing or the machine running unusually hot.

Can a dirty blower wheel start a fire?

Yes. Lint packed around the blower wheel restricts airflow, which causes heat to build inside the cabinet. That's one of the primary internal ignition sources the U.S. Fire Administration tracks — separate from vent duct fires that most people think of first.

My dryer vent was just cleaned. Why is it still slow?

Vent cleaning addresses the exhaust duct from the cabinet to the outside wall. It does nothing to the internal blower wheel or lint trap slot. If the vent is clear and the dryer is still slow, the restriction is almost certainly inside the machine — and that's where we look first.

Is dryer lint trap cleaning enough if I do it every load?

Cleaning the screen every load is the right habit, but it only captures the lint large enough to be caught by the mesh. Finer particles pass through and accumulate in the slot and blower housing over time. Screen cleaning alone will not prevent internal buildup.

title: Ice maker died again? It's probably not the ice maker.
excerpt: Ice maker not making ice? The problem is usually the water valve or filter — not the ice maker itself. Here's what to check first, from My Appliance Repair in Connecticut.
author: Elmir R.
content:
Last spring I got a call from a guy in Branford who had already ordered a $200 ice maker assembly off Amazon. It was sitting on his counter in the box when I got there. The water inlet valve was clogged. He sent the assembly back unopened.

This is the most common version of the ice-maker-not-making-ice story. The ice maker gets blamed because it's the visible thing, the thing with a name, the thing that stopped doing its job. But on most service calls here in Connecticut, the ice maker is the victim, not the cause. Before you order anything or call anyone, run through the checklist below.

Quick checklist: why your ice maker stopped making ice

These are the seven most common reasons an ice maker stops making ice — roughly in order of how often we see them on service calls across Connecticut.

Most likely causes

  • Water inlet valve clogged or failing
  • Water filter overdue for replacement
  • Freezer temperature running too warm
  • Kinked or frozen water supply line
  • Low household water pressure
  • Bail arm stuck in the off position
  • Ice maker module or mold thermostat failure

Most of these take ten minutes to check yourself. Here's what to look for on each one.

The water inlet valve: the first place to look

The water inlet valve is a small electrically controlled valve that opens to let water into the ice maker. They wear out, they clog with mineral deposits, and when they fail the ice maker either cycles through its routine and produces nothing, or makes those thin hollow cubes that fall apart when you touch them. Valve replacement runs $40 to $80 in parts depending on the brand — a long way from a full ice maker assembly.

Classic symptom: Ice maker not making ice, but you can hear it cycling — nothing comes out. That's almost always the inlet valve, not the module.

A lot of the time the module is fine and the valve isn't opening fully. This is the first thing we check on a service call, and it's the first thing you should check at home.

The water filter nobody's touched in three years

Before you call anyone, go find your water filter. If you can't remember when you changed it last, change it now. A clogged filter creates enough flow restriction to starve the ice maker, and the result looks exactly like a hardware failure: no drama, no error code, just no ice.

About half the people I talk to don't know where their filter is, or didn't know the fridge had one. Some in-door filter housings hide them pretty well. A few things worth knowing:

  • Most manufacturers recommend replacement every six months
  • Once a year is realistic for most Connecticut households
  • Three years is not fine — and it's one of the most common reasons we find for ice maker not making ice on service calls

Freezer temperature and water pressure

Ice makers have a built-in cutoff. If the freezer runs above roughly 10°F, the ice maker shuts itself off. That's actually it working correctly — protecting itself from making a mess. So if your freezer is running warm because the evaporator fan is struggling or the door gasket has been leaking cold air for the last eight months, the ice maker isn't broken. It's just waiting for conditions that aren't coming.

Check your freezer temp with a cheap thermometer before assuming anything. If it's reading 18 or 20 degrees, a warm freezer — not a broken ice maker — is why you're not getting ice.

Water pressure is worth checking at the same time. Manufacturers typically require at least 20 PSI at the valve. A quick way to test it: dispense water into a measuring cup for ten seconds — you should get at least six ounces. If you come up short, remove the water filter and try again. A clogged filter is often the culprit, but if pressure is still low without it, the issue may be further upstream.

Check the water line behind the fridge

This one takes ten minutes. Pull the fridge out and look at the water line. Kinked lines are more common than they should be, especially after someone slid the fridge back in a hurry. And in older Connecticut homes where kitchen plumbing runs near an exterior wall, that line can freeze in a bad winter. We've seen this in Waterbury and New Haven a handful of times, usually in January. It thaws out, works fine, nobody ever knew.

Samsung, Whirlpool, and LG ice makers: what's different

The checklist above applies to most refrigerator brands, but a few are worth calling out specifically:

  • Samsung: The French door models have a well-documented ice maker freezing problem — the ice maker itself freezes over and stops cycling. This is a design issue, not user error, and it requires defrosting the unit and in some cases a duct cover fix.
  • Whirlpool / Maytag: The modular ice maker design on many side-by-side models has a common mold thermostat failure point. Worth testing before replacing the full assembly.
  • LG: Certain LG models with the craft ice feature have had known issues with the lower ice maker. If your LG is producing no ice at all, check for a software or sensor issue before assuming mechanical failure.

If you're not sure what you're dealing with, brand-specific diagnosis is part of what My Appliance Repair does on every service call across Connecticut.

When the ice maker itself is actually the problem

It does happen. The bail arm gets stuck in the off position, the mold thermostat fails, the motor burns out. If you need the full assembly replaced on a Samsung or Whirlpool, you're looking at $150 to $250 in parts plus labor. That's a reasonable fix on a fridge that's under eight or ten years old. On a fifteen-year-old unit, the conversation gets more complicated — and at My Appliance Repair, we'll tell you that honestly before you spend anything.

You can take a look at our appliance repair services to get a sense of what we cover. If you want a straight answer about whether something's worth fixing, just contact our team and we'll give you an honest assessment before any money changes hands.

But do the easy stuff first. Filter, temperature, water pressure, water line. Half the time you've already solved the ice-maker-not-making-ice problem before anyone shows up. If you haven't, book a service call with My Appliance Repair and we'll start with the valve — not the part you already ordered off Amazon.

title: Stacking your washer and dryer is probably voiding your warranty
excerpt: Stacking your washer and dryer without the right kit voids warranties and wears out drum bearings. What Connecticut homeowners need to know.
author: Elmir R.
content:
Stacking Your Washer and Dryer Is Probably Voiding Your Warranty

Stacking a washer and dryer seems like the obvious solution when you're working with a laundry closet, a finished basement, or a condo with thirty-six inches of floor space. But done without the correct manufacturer-approved stacking kit, it can void your warranty, accelerate drum bearing wear, and quietly destroy a control board — all before you notice anything is wrong. If you're in Connecticut and you've stacked your machines without the right stacking kit, this post is for you.

Last spring I got a call out to Naugatuck — a couple in a condo who'd been stacking their laundry for two years on a piece of plywood they'd cut to fit. Front-load washer on the bottom, top-load dryer sitting on top. I'm not joking about the plywood. The dryer drum was so worn out of round I could see it wobbling through the door glass. They had no idea any of this was connected to how they'd set the machines up.

This is more common than I'd like to admit — not always the plywood, but the general situation. People stacking their washer and dryer without thinking too hard about it, assuming that if it physically fits, it's fine. It's not fine. And beyond the mechanical damage, it may already be costing you a warranty claim you don't know you've lost yet.

Why so many Connecticut homeowners end up stacking in the first place

Laundry closets. Finished basements with low ceilings. Condos where the builder gave you thirty-six inches of floor space and called it a laundry room. Stacking is just the obvious move when you're working with a tight footprint, and appliance manufacturers know this — which is exactly why they make stacking kits. They'd rather sell you the stacking kit than have you rig something up.

Most people skip the kit entirely. Or they buy a generic shelf-style bracket they found online for twelve dollars. Or they do the plywood thing. The manufacturer-approved stacking kit for most Whirlpool and LG front-loaders runs somewhere between thirty and sixty dollars depending on where you source it. It's designed specifically to lock the dryer to the washer frame so vibration doesn't transfer the way it otherwise would. That's the whole job the stacking kit does. It's not complicated, but skipping it is how you turn a five-year-old dryer into a three-year-old dryer.

Brand compatibility: Whirlpool, LG, and why mixing brands matters

Whirlpool and LG are the two brands I see stacking problems on the most, partly because their stacking requirements are buried deep in the installation manual — not on the first page, not on a sticker on the unit. You have to go looking. So people don't find it, they stack the washer and dryer without the kit, and six months later the dryer starts making a low rumble that slowly gets worse.

Not all front-loaders are rated to stack together, even within the same brand. Mixing brands — say, a Whirlpool washer under an LG dryer — is almost always a problem. The mounting geometry is different, the vibration damping assumptions are different, and no manufacturer-approved stacking kit exists to bridge that gap. If the model numbers don't match the stacking kit, you don't have a supported installation.

The mechanical damage from improper stacking

What's actually happening inside the machines

The spin cycle on the washer sends vibration up into the dryer. Without the stacking kit creating a rigid connection, the dryer just absorbs that energy through its feet. Over time this accelerates wear on the drum bearings. I've also seen it travel into the dryer's control board — twice in the last year I diagnosed a control board failure and traced it directly back to vibration from an improperly stacked setup. Control boards are a much more expensive problem than drum bearings.

None of this requires a dramatic failure to be doing damage. It's slow, cumulative wear that shows up on a service call two years later and looks like a random breakdown.

Why leveling matters more when the units are stacked

One unlevel unit throws off both of them. I say this on basically every stacked-setup call I go on. People level the bottom unit, set the dryer on top, and assume they're done. But the stacking kit and the leveling legs work together. If the whole column is slightly off, the washer rocks during spin, the dryer rocks with it, and now you've got two machines doing something they shouldn't be doing.

Check the level after you install the stacking kit. Both units — not just the washer.

The warranty part nobody expects

Here's where it gets genuinely frustrating. Most major brands will ask about installation before honoring a warranty claim on a washer or dryer — how it's set up, whether it's stacked, what kit was used. "Improper installation" is a real denial reason, and stacking a washer and dryer without the correct manufacturer-approved stacking kit qualifies.

I had a customer in Meriden who'd paid for an extended warranty on both her machines. She called me after two previous repair visits from someone else hadn't solved a rattling problem. Turned out the washer was shaking the entire column and the dryer was showing the symptoms. The extended warranty had already denied one claim. She was on her own by the time I got there.

She'd bought that warranty in good faith. Paid real money for it. And the improper stacking setup had voided her coverage before anything ever went wrong. Nobody told her that at the store.

Common questions about stacking kits and warranty coverage

Does stacking always void the warranty?

Not automatically — but stacking without the correct manufacturer-approved stacking kit gives the manufacturer grounds to deny a claim related to mechanical wear or vibration damage. If they ask how the unit was installed and it wasn't done to spec, that's a real exposure. Using the right kit for your specific model pair keeps you covered.

Can I stack a Whirlpool dryer on a different brand's washer?

Almost never with a manufacturer-supported kit. Cross-brand stacking — a Whirlpool dryer on an LG washer, for example — typically has no approved stacking kit, which means no supported installation exists. Even if the units are physically close in size, the mounting geometry and vibration tolerances are designed as matched pairs. Mixing brands is one of the faster ways to end up with an unresolvable warranty situation.

How do I know if my models are compatible for stacking?

The model number sticker is inside the door frame on both units. Take both model numbers, pull up the installation guide on the manufacturer's website, and look for the stacking compatibility list. If a specific stacking kit part number is listed for your model pair, you're in good shape. If it isn't listed at all, the units likely aren't rated to stack together.

What does a stacking kit actually cost?

Most manufacturer-approved stacking kits for Whirlpool, LG, Maytag, and Samsung front-loaders run between thirty and seventy dollars. That's the part alone — a fraction of what a drum bearing replacement or a control board costs, which is typically where improper stacking ends up.

Can I fix an improperly stacked setup myself?

In many cases, yes — if your model pair is rated to stack and you can source the correct stacking kit. The installation usually involves attaching a bracket that locks the dryer feet to the washer top panel. The harder part is re-leveling both units correctly after the kit goes in. If you're not confident in the leveling or you're already hearing noise, it's worth having a technician check the machines before you reassemble the stack.

If you're already stacked, here's what to actually do

Don't panic — most situations are fixable. Here's the order I recommend:

  • Confirm your models are rated to stack together. Not all front-loaders are, even within the same brand, and mixing brands is almost always a problem. The model numbers are on a sticker inside the door frame. Look them up, find the installation guide, and check stacking compatibility. This takes ten minutes and it matters.
  • Get the right manufacturer-approved stacking kit. Appliance parts suppliers usually carry them. At My Appliance Repair we can typically source the correct stacking kit within a day or two. You can see more about our appliance repair services if you're not sure what you're dealing with.
  • Re-level both units from scratch after the kit goes in. Don't assume the floor is doing the work. Adjust the leveling legs on the washer first, then confirm the dryer is plumb at the top of the stack.
  • Listen for anything new. If a noise started right after stacking, something was likely already worn before the stack went up. Don't wait — book a service call before the problem reaches parts that cost real money.

One situation where unstacking is the right answer

If one of your machines is significantly older than the other, think hard before stacking a new unit on top of a worn-out one. A washer that's already vibrating more than it should — because the drum bearings are going or the shock absorbers are tired — is going to punish whatever's sitting on top of it.

In cases like that, the honest recommendation is to unstack, address the worn machine, and then re-stack correctly with the proper stacking kit. It costs more upfront but it's cheaper than replacing a dryer control board six months from now.

Get your stacked laundry setup checked by a Connecticut appliance repair tech

If any of this sounds like your setup, My Appliance Repair services Naugatuck, Meriden, Waterbury, New Haven, Bridgeport, Middletown, and communities throughout Connecticut. It usually takes about ten minutes on-site to tell you whether the stack is the problem — and most of the time we can source the right stacking kit and correct the installation in the same visit.

Book a service call online, or contact our team if you have questions before scheduling. We'd rather help you get the setup right than come back later for a drum bearing job.

title: Leaving food in your fridge when the power goes out costs you more than you think
excerpt: Power outage refrigerator food safety starts with one rule: keep the door closed. What to save, what to toss, and how to protect your fridge — from a Connecticut repair team.
author: Elmir R.
content:
A woman in Meriden called us after a storm last spring. Power had been out for about eight hours, and she'd opened the fridge maybe five or six times to check on things. "Just a quick look," she kept saying. She lost everything — and with basic power outage refrigerator food safety knowledge, she didn't have to lose any of it.

That call happens more than you'd think. So here's what the team at My Appliance Repair tells people standing in their kitchen the day after a Connecticut storm — because it saves food, and sometimes it saves your compressor.

How long your refrigerator actually stays safe during a power outage

The four-hour window

A closed refrigerator holds a safe temperature for roughly four hours during a power outage. A packed freezer can hold it for a full day or two. The word that matters in both of those sentences is closed.

Every time you open the door you're letting cold air fall out and warm air pour in. It's not dramatic — it just adds up fast. Five "quick looks" over eight hours and you've blown the whole window. The fridge can't tell you whether your leftovers are okay by you staring at them. A thermometer can. Most people don't own one. A basic refrigerator thermometer runs about six dollars and is worth having before you need it.

If the outage is going to run long

If it looks like power won't be back within a few hours, move what matters most into a cooler with ice before the four-hour mark — don't wait until after. Prioritize:

  • Deli meat and opened packages of poultry or fish
  • Opened dairy — milk, cream, soft cheeses
  • Anything already cooked
  • Items with eggs or mayo

Leave condiments where they are. More on that below.

Power outage refrigerator food safety: what to throw out and what to keep

The core rule for power outage refrigerator food safety is 40°F. If your fridge has been above that temperature for more than two hours, certain things have to go. No exceptions:

  • Cooked meat, poultry, and fish
  • Cut fruit and leafy greens
  • Soft cheeses and opened dairy
  • Anything with eggs in it — casseroles, quiche, custards
  • Opened mayo and creamy dressings
  • Leftover takeout

Condiments are more forgiving than people think. Ketchup, mustard, pickles, hard cheeses, butter, and whole fruits and vegetables are not the things that get you sick. It's cooked proteins and dairy-heavy items you need to be honest about.

If you don't have a thermometer and you're guessing — that's exactly what it is. A guess. Food poisoning from spoiled chicken is not a fun way to spend a Tuesday.

Freezer food safety: what the rules are after a power outage

Everyone asks the same thing: "Is it still frozen?" And they want the answer to be yes. The real question is whether it partially thawed and refroze, because that's what actually causes problems.

  • Safe: Meat that's still cold and firm all the way to the center.
  • Discard: Anything soft in the middle, or with visible pooled liquid in the bag — that refroze.

Ice crystals on the surface don't tell you much. "Still has some ice on it" is not the same as "safe to eat." The freezer is more forgiving than the fridge during a power outage, but it has limits too.

The fridge damage that shows up two days later

This is the part no food safety guide covers, because they're not written by appliance technicians. Power coming back isn't always gentle. Voltage spikes on restore hit your refrigerator's electrical components hard — especially the start relay and the control board.

We got a call in Waterbury last winter, two days after a big storm. Three-year-old Samsung, completely dead. Compressor not running, not cold. The customer had a surge protector on his TV, his router, his gaming setup — nothing on the fridge. The control board was fried. That was a $280 repair. A decent surge protector for an appliance outlet runs about $25.

Parts most likely to fail after a power outage

  • Start relay: $40–$80 for the part. One of the most common failures we see after outage events.
  • Control board: $200 or more on newer Samsung and LG units with advanced electronics.
  • Compressor: Less common, but voltage irregularities on restore can stress it over time.

If your refrigerator is plugged into a plain wall outlet with no surge protection right now, that's the single easiest thing you can change before the next storm hits Connecticut.

What to do after the power comes back on

Give the compressor time to stabilize

Wait 15 to 20 minutes before loading food back into the refrigerator. Let the compressor cycle up and stabilize. Listen for it — a healthy compressor starts up, runs for a bit, then goes quiet. It should do that several times in the first hour.

Signs something is wrong

If the compressor is running constantly and the temperature isn't dropping, that's a problem. Either the compressor is struggling or something in the sealed system took damage. Watch the temp over the next two to three hours. If it's not back down to the mid-30s by then, stop loading food into it and call someone.

At My Appliance Repair, we're happy to help you figure out what you're dealing with before you commit to a service visit. Contact our team and describe what you're hearing — we can usually tell you over the phone whether it warrants a visit or whether the unit just needs more time to recover. We'd rather spend two minutes on a call than have you throw out another fridge full of food unnecessarily.

Before the next Connecticut storm: your power outage refrigerator food safety checklist

Connecticut storm season runs from spring thunderstorms straight through to nor'easters in late fall. Good power outage refrigerator food safety habits start before the outage — not during it. Here's the short list:

  • Put a $6 refrigerator thermometer inside your fridge today
  • Plug your refrigerator into a surge-protected outlet
  • Keep a cooler and ice packs on hand during storm season
  • Resist the urge to open the door during an outage
  • Know your four-hour window — and act before it closes
